name: Full-Thickness Rotator Cuff Tear
summary: Complete disruption through the tendon thickness, ranging from degenerative tears with preserved function to acute traumatic tears with major weakness.

looksLike: Possible pseudoparalysis after acute major tear
redFlags: Acute traumatic inability to elevate arm
firstSteps: Orthopaedic referral for acute traumatic full-thickness tears, pseudoparalysis or major functional loss
Discuss goals, age, tendon quality, tear size and functional demand

assess: Pain may be surprisingly modest in some chronic tears

tests.name: External Rotation Lag Sign
tests.purpose: Assess posterior cuff integrity, especially infraspinatus.
tests.positive: Patient cannot maintain the externally rotated position and the arm drifts inward.

tests.name: Drop Arm Test
tests.purpose: Assess ability to eccentrically control shoulder elevation.
tests.positive: Arm drops suddenly or patient cannot control lowering because of weakness.

tests.name: Lift-Off / Belly Press
tests.positive: Unable/weak lift-off, or elbow falls backward/wrist flexes during belly press.

differentials: Rotator cuff tendinopathy without major tear

stages.label: Determine Surgical vs Nonsurgical Pathway
stages.goal: Identify acute traumatic tears or major weakness that merit orthopaedic opinion.
do: Orthopaedic referral for acute traumatic full-thickness tears, pseudoparalysis or major functional loss
Discuss goals, age, tendon quality, tear size and functional demand
dose: Maintain comfortable ROM and low-load activation while awaiting plan if safe

stages.label: Nonsurgical Capacity / Prehab
stages.goal: Improve pain, motion and remaining cuff/deltoid/scapular capacity.

stages.label: Functional Strength
stages.goal: Maximize usable strength and overhead capacity where appropriate.
moveOn: Task-specific function satisfactory without worsening weakness

returnCriteria: Depends on nonsurgical vs post-repair pathway

structures: Infraspinatus and subscapularis may be involved
classification: Small/medium/large/massive based on imaging and involved tendons
investigations: Ultrasound or MRI is useful when a major tear is suspected and results may change management.
manual: Use only to address painful stiffness or secondary mobility deficits.
Do not imply manual therapy can heal a full-thickness tendon defect.
After surgical repair, follow surgeon-specific protection before manual techniques.
modalities: Symptom-relieving modalities may be adjuncts only.
Exercise or surgical decision-making should not be delayed in major traumatic weakness by repeated passive modalities.
mistakes: Treating acute pseudoparalysis as simple impingement
pearls: Large traumatic weakness + lag/drop-arm signs deserves timely imaging/referral.
Pain severity alone does not indicate tear size.

tests.name: External Rotation Lag Sign
tests.purpose: Assess posterior cuff integrity, especially infraspinatus.
tests.positive: Patient cannot maintain the externally rotated position and the arm drifts inward.
tests.patientPosition: Sitting/standing with elbow flexed; shoulder placed near end-range external rotation.
tests.handPlacement: One hand positions the wrist/forearm; the other may stabilize elbow.
procedure: Passively place shoulder into external rotation.
Ask patient to maintain position when support is released.
Observe any lag toward internal rotation.
tests.interpretation: Raises suspicion of significant posterior rotator cuff tear.

tests.name: Drop Arm Test
tests.purpose: Assess ability to eccentrically control shoulder elevation.
tests.positive: Arm drops suddenly or patient cannot control lowering because of weakness.
tests.patientPosition: Standing/sitting with arm passively or actively abducted.
tests.handPlacement: Support arm as needed to start.
procedure: Ask patient to slowly lower it.
tests.interpretation: Supports a large rotator cuff tear when consistent with history.

tests.name: Lift-Off / Belly Press
tests.positive: Unable/weak lift-off, or elbow falls backward/wrist flexes during belly press.
tests.handPlacement: For lift-off, patient places dorsum of hand on low back; for belly press, palm on abdomen.
procedure: Lift-off: ask patient to move hand away from back.
Belly press: ask patient to press abdomen while keeping elbow forward and wrist neutral.

story.headline: The shoulder that could be lifted—but couldn't lift itself
story.scene: An older gardener falls onto an outstretched arm. A family member can gently help raise his arm, yet he cannot actively lift it well. 'I thought a torn muscle must always hurt terribly,' he says.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'Pain is only moderate, so the damage can't be big?' Therapist: 'Pain volume is not an MRI report.'
story.clue: After trauma, disproportionate active weakness or an inability to elevate the arm despite more passive motion raises concern for a major cuff tear.
story.twist: The size of a tear and the level of pain do not correlate neatly. Acute traumatic weakness deserves timely medical evaluation rather than waiting through weeks of generic exercises.
story.aha: Active-versus-passive movement tells a clinical story that pain intensity alone cannot.
story.patientTranslation: The tendons that help lift and rotate your shoulder may have torn. Because this followed a fall with significant weakness, a clinician should assess whether imaging or specialist treatment is needed.
story.clinicianReasoning: Differentiate traumatic cuff tear from fracture, dislocation, nerve injury and pain inhibition. Examine active/passive range, strength, lag signs and neurovascular status; refer promptly for acute traumatic functional loss.
story.rehabBridge: Select a pathway after assessment. Nonoperative or postoperative rehabilitation emphasizes protected movement and staged strengthening according to the injury and restrictions.
story.question: After a fall, active elevation is profoundly weak but gentle passive elevation is more available. Which is most appropriate?
options: Timely assessment for acute traumatic cuff tear and associated injury
Diagnose adhesive capsulitis from one finding
Force overhead strengthening on day one
story.explanation: Major new weakness after trauma raises concern for an acute tear or other serious injury; timely medical assessment is appropriate.
